title: B-TREES AND B+ TREES
subtitle: Page-sized nodes full of keys: a few disk reads find any key among billions.
footer: System Design, Step by Step · core concepts

blocks.text: Each page holds boundary keys; follow the range that contains your key. Branching factor ~500 → 3–4 levels for billions of keys.
B+ trees keep values only in linked leaves: more keys per internal page, shallower tree, cheap range scans. Databases use B+ trees.
Full leaf → two half-full pages + a new boundary key in the parent. Only a root split adds a level. Every change goes through the WAL.
Descend once, then walk the linked leaves. Results come out sorted, so ORDER BY and LIMIT are free.

items: Random UUIDv4 keys scatter inserts and splits; prefer time-ordered IDs
Writes are random page overwrites: LSM-trees win for write-heavy loads
InnoDB: rows live in the primary-key B+ tree (clustered)

blocks.text: "Postgres indexes are B+ trees: about three page reads per lookup, and the date-range query is one index range scan along the linked leaves. I'd use time-ordered IDs so inserts append instead of splitting pages everywhere."
